content: Zidovudine, one of the components of COMBIVIR, has been linked to hematologic toxicity, including neutropenia and anemia, particularly in individuals with advanced HIV-1 infection. Caution is advised when prescribing COMBIVIR to patients with compromised bone marrow, as indicated by a granulocyte count below 1,000 cells/mm³ or hemoglobin levels under 9.5 g/dL. For patients with advanced HIV-1, frequent blood count monitoring is strongly recommended, while periodic blood counts are advised for other HIV-1-infected individuals. If anemia or neutropenia develops, it may be necessary to interrupt the dosage. Prolonged use of zidovudine has been associated with myopathy and myositis, which exhibit pathological changes similar to those caused by HIV-1 infection. These conditions may also occur during treatment with COMBIVIR. Lactic acidosis and hepatomegaly with steatosis, including fatal cases, have been reported in patients treated with nucleoside analogues such as lamivudine and zidovudine, either alone or in combination with other antiretrovirals. Patients with known risk factors for liver disease should be treated with COMBIVIR cautiously, although these conditions have also been reported in individuals without identifiable risk factors. If clinical or laboratory findings suggest lactic acidosis or significant hepatotoxicity, including hepatomegaly or steatosis, treatment with COMBIVIR should be discontinued. In patients co-infected with HIV-1 and hepatitis B virus (HBV), discontinuation of lamivudine has been associated with exacerbations of hepatitis, as evidenced by elevated serum ALT levels and the re-emergence of HBV DNA. While most cases are self-limiting, fatalities have been reported. Patients should be closely monitored clinically and through laboratory tests for several months after stopping treatment. The safety and efficacy of lamivudine for treating chronic hepatitis B in patients co-infected with HIV-1 and HBV have not been established. Additionally, the emergence of lamivudine-resistant HBV has been observed in both HIV-1-infected and non-HIV-infected patients, which may reduce treatment efficacy. COMBIVIR is a fixed-dose combination of lamivudine and zidovudine and should not be used alongside other products containing lamivudine, zidovudine, or emtricitabine. Examples include EPIVIR, EPIVIR-HBV, RETROVIR, EPZICOM, TRIZIVIR, ATRIPLA, EMTRIVA, and TRUVADA. Ribavirin has been shown in vitro to reduce the phosphorylation of pyrimidine nucleoside analogues like lamivudine and zidovudine. Although no pharmacokinetic or pharmacodynamic interactions have been observed in co-infected HIV-1/HCV patients, hepatic decompensation, including fatal cases, has occurred in patients receiving combination antiretroviral therapy with interferon alfa, with or without ribavirin. Patients on COMBIVIR and interferon alfa, with or without ribavirin, should be closely monitored for toxicities such as hepatic decompensation, neutropenia, and anemia. If clinical toxicities worsen, discontinuation of COMBIVIR, interferon alfa, ribavirin, or a combination of these should be considered. Co-administration of ribavirin and zidovudine is not recommended due to reports of exacerbated anemia in co-infected patients. COMBIVIR should be used cautiously in patients with a history of pancreatitis or significant risk factors for developing pancreatitis. If clinical signs, symptoms, or laboratory abnormalities suggestive of pancreatitis occur, treatment with COMBIVIR should be discontinued immediately. Immune reconstitution syndrome has been reported in patients undergoing combination antiretroviral therapy, including COMBIVIR. During the initial phase of treatment, patients with improving immune systems may develop inflammatory responses to latent or residual opportunistic infections, such as Mycobacterium avium, cytomegalovirus, Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, or tuberculosis. These conditions may require further evaluation and treatment. Redistribution or accumulation of body fat has been observed in patients receiving antiretroviral therapy. Manifestations include central obesity, dorsocervical fat enlargement (buffalo hump), peripheral wasting, facial wasting, breast enlargement, and a Cushingoid appearance. The mechanism and long-term consequences of these changes remain unclear, and a direct causal relationship has not been established.
